1.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The opening that is most often quoted in Beatles harmonic trivia is the
I – v / I – bV leap that opens the string introduction to Eleanor Rigby/A
Hard Day’s Night material.

In the guise in which it is usually taught the move is heard as a
tonic major/minor  i  → v  leap.  In E minor / G major the intro is
literally

E minor – B minor   /   G major – E minor

i → v, i.e. tonic to the minor-fifth / minor dominant chord, a perfect-fifth
root move which is the textbook “tonic to the minor fifth chord” opening.
The same interval class is the one that is made famous in popular writing
as the big opening jump of A Hard Day’s Night, the G-major tonic that
immediately jumps to the v-minor  E-minor / the tritone-coloured
second chord of the A Hard Day’s Night introduction. That is the
Beatles I→v / tonic-to-minor-fifth jump that is normally cited in the
literature. 

The classic popular version of the tritone/tonic-to-bV form of the same
idea is the opening of Come Together / A Day in the Life, where the
tonic major is immediately answered by the chord a tritone/minor-fifth
away from it, the move that most listeners remember as the Beatles’
characteristic opening leap.

5.text:
In the parlance of pop analysis the thing that is normally meant by a
“minor fifth chord” is the fifth-degree triad of a major key being
spelled minor, i.e. the v chord, and in the minor mode the same i → v
motion. 

The textbook example in a major key is the opening twin-guitar riff of
*Revolver – And Your Bird Can Sing*.  The song is in E major and the
verse riff is built on

    E – Bm – E – Bm…

the first two sonorities being the tonic E major and the diatonic fifth
degree spelled as B minor, the v chord, in E major. In root position
that is the perfect-fifth jump

    E  →  B

I → v, the conventional I–v opening that gives the riff its slightly
unsettled, Beatles-modal colour. 

The same i → v motion is the string-quartet opening of the minor-mode
*Eleanor Rigby*, A minor – E minor, i – v, which is the minor-mode
realisation of the same tonic-to-minor-fifth idea.

2.text:
The tritone / I – bV opening that is normally talked about in Beatles writing is
the one that is quoted for the Walrus.  

The verse is normally analysed in F. The piano / guitar bed opens on the
tonic F major and, on the second beat of the bar, the music jumps a
diminished 5th / minor 5th, i.e. a tritone, to the chord built on the
flat 5th of the tonic, Db major. F → Db is the textbook tonic-to-flat-fifth,
tonic-to-minor-fifth, jump that gives the number its famously unsettled
opening. The same kind of I→♭V / I→v tritone jump is the one that is
repeatedly cited for the opening of Come Together / I Want You - She's So
Heavy and, in the more conventional I→v reading, e.g. E→Bm at the start of
Back in the U.S.S.R., which is the I-to-minor-fifth-degree move that is
usually meant in popular writing.

3.text:
The classic I – v opening that is usually quoted in that context is the
E-major opening of Norwegian Wood (This Bird Has Flown).

The song is in E major. The sitar/piano intro is stated on the tonic
E major and the very next harmonic area is the v, the minor fifth
degree. In E major

    I  =  E – G♯ – B
    v  =  B – D – F♯

i.e. B minor a perfect 5th below the tonic. The opening statement is
the textbook tonic → minor-fifth jump E major → B minor, the v chord
in the key, the jump that gives the verse its slightly uneasy, modal
colour. That I – v inflection is the one that is normally pointed to
in Beatles trivia – in a minor-key reading the same inflection is
heard as the i – v opening of Eleanor Rigby, Em → Bm, the minor-key
analogue of the same tonic-to-minor-fifth move.
